title: Vomiting and drowsiness in a 15-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes
desc: In this station the candidate takes a focused history from the mother of Sasha, a 15-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes, and examines Sasha in the ED. Sasha has vomited three times this evening and was found on the floor, drowsy and confused. The candidate then interprets her observations, arterial blood gas, blood results and urine dipstick, and gives the diagnosis and differentials. They outline ED management following the RCH guideline, then explain to her mother what has happened, what the nurses will watch for and what follow-up Sasha needs.
focus: Vomiting and a reduced conscious state in an adolescent with type 1 diabetes: recognising diabetic ketoacidosis, managing it safely with the risk of cerebral oedema in mind, and finding the psychosocial cause
stem: You are a junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital, in the evening. Sasha, a 15-year-old girl, has been brought in by her mother, Celine. Sasha has vomited several times this evening, and Celine found her on the floor at home, drowsy and confused. Sasha is too drowsy to give a history herself. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Celine and perform a focused examination of Sasha, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Sasha's observations, her arterial blood gas, her blood results and a urine dipstick. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer Celine's question (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Celine, Sasha's mother. Sasha is 15 and lies on the trolley with her eyes closed. You stand beside her, frightened and talking quickly. You answer the history for Sasha and give each detail only when asked. The examiner voices Sasha's few words (below) and gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “Sasha's been vomiting since this evening. I found her on the floor just completely out of it – she can barely string a sentence together.”

The vomiting (give only when asked)

  • Onset: sudden, this evening.
  • How often: 3 vomits over a few hours.
  • What it looks like: “Normal-looking vomit”, yellow with bits of food. If asked: no blood, and not green.
  • Amount: not much each time.
  • Better or worse: nothing changes it.
  • Before: she has had gastro in the past, but never anything like this.
  • If asked about drinking and dehydration: “She's definitely been thirstier for a few days, and a bit off.”

How she is now (only when asked)

  • You found her on the floor of her bedroom this evening, confused. “She can't even open her eyes to speak to me.”
  • No injury that you could see. As far as you know she didn't hit her head.
  • If asked about tablets or alcohol tonight: she has been at home all evening. You don't think she has had anything to drink tonight, and no tablets are missing as far as you know.
  • If asked about headache: she hasn't mentioned one; she has only complained of her tummy.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • Tummy: she has been complaining of tummy pain “all over”, and it is hard to get her to say more. No diarrhoea and no change in her bowels.
  • Urine: she has been passing a lot of urine and drinking a lot. No stinging or burning, and no pain in her back or sides.
  • General: tired, and she has lost weight lately (her clothes are looser). No fever, no runny nose or cough.
  • Infection: “Maybe she has caught something off her friends? There's a bug going around at school, but she doesn't have a fever.” No travel, and no food that could have been off.
  • Medicines: no changes, and no steroids.
  • Sexual activity: not sexually active as far as you know.
  • Periods: regular, last one about 2 weeks ago, as far as you know.

Her diabetes (only when asked)

  • Type 1 diabetes since she was 12. She takes NovoMix insulin twice a day and does her own injections now.
  • If asked whether she has been taking her insulin: “I'm meant to keep an eye on it, but she does it herself now. Her sister told me she's been skipping doses because she wants to lose weight. I didn't know what to do.” You don't know when her last dose was, and you don't think she had it this morning.
  • If asked about her control or HbA1c: her HbA1c was 9% at the GP 3 weeks ago.
  • If asked about alcohol: she drinks at parties.

Background (only when asked)

  • Past history: type 1 diabetes since 12. Appendix out at 14.
  • Medications: NovoMix twice a day. Nothing else.
  • Allergies: none that you know of.
  • Family history: you have Hashimoto's thyroid disease, and Sasha's sister has coeliac disease. Nobody else has type 1 diabetes.
  • Social: she is in Year 9 and has been more stressed lately, with problems in her friendship group. She lives with you and her sister, and there have been more arguments at home recently. She drinks alcohol occasionally. She doesn't smoke or take drugs as far as you know.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: she has caught the bug going around school.
  • Concern: “I'm just worried it is something serious.”
  • Expectation: you want someone to help her now and to tell you what is wrong.
  • Question to raise once: “Is she going to be all right?” A good candidate is honest that she is very unwell, and says the team is treating her now and will explain once the tests are back.

Sasha (voiced by the examiner)

  • If spoken to loudly, she opens her eyes briefly and mumbles: “My tummy hurts… I'm so thirsty.” She does not know where she is.
  • She obeys simple commands (squeezes a hand) but drifts off again.
  • If asked whether her head hurts, she mumbles: “No… just my tummy.”

The nurse and how Sasha changes

  • If asked for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 38 (deep, sighing breaths), SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/70, HR 142 regular, temperature 36.8 °C, responds to voice, CRT 2 seconds. Weight 48 kg.
  • If asked for a bedside glucose: 22.0 mmol/L. If asked for a bedside ketone: 5.3 mmol/L.
  • If the candidate asks for senior help or to move Sasha to the resuscitation bay, the nurse says: “Moving her now, the consultant's on her way.”
  • If the candidate asks for IV access, bloods, a blood gas or a urine sample, the nurse arranges them, and the examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.
  • If the candidate orders fluids, insulin or any other treatment, the nurse acknowledges it and the examiner says: “Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2.”
  • Partway through the history, the nurse says: “She's vomited again, only a small amount, and she's still breathing very deeply.”
  • Sasha's conscious level does not change during Part 1, whatever the candidate does.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • Observations: as the nurse gives above. Weight 48 kg.
  • General: thin teenage girl, eyes closed, rouses to voice, confused. Her breath smells sweet, like nail polish remover (acetone).
  • Conscious level: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive to light. Moves all four limbs equally. No focal neurological signs.
  • Head: no bruising, swelling or scalp wound.
  • Hydration and perfusion: dry lips and tongue, sunken eyes. CRT 2 seconds, warm hands and feet, radial pulses of good volume.
  • Breathing: deep, rapid, regular breathing without recession or added sounds. Equal air entry and a clear chest.
  • Heart: tachycardic, dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen: three small, healed laparoscopic scars. Soft, mildly tender all over, no guarding or rebound tenderness. No masses. Bowel sounds present. Renal angles not tender.
  • Infection screen: no neck stiffness. No rash and no petechiae. Ears and throat normal.
  • Everything else is normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self to Celine (and to Sasha), confirms Sasha's identity and Celine's relationship to her, and explains that Sasha will be assessed while the history is taken.

Recognises early that Sasha is seriously unwell and acts before the history is finished: asks the nurse for a full set of observations with a bedside glucose and ketone, and asks for senior help and a move to the resuscitation bay.
check.d: Also credit asking at this point for IV access, bloods and a blood gas. The critical element is checking the bedside glucose and ketone early.

check.x: Acknowledges Celine's fear with empathy, uses plain language, and asks about the missed insulin without judging Sasha or Celine.
History
Characterises the vomiting:

kids.x: Onset and frequency: sudden this evening, 3 vomits over a few hours
Content: yellow with bits of food; asks specifically about blood and green (bilious) vomit (none)
Volume and hydration: small amounts each time; thirstier for a few days and 'a bit off'
Past episodes and modifying factors: gastro before but never like this; nothing changes it

check.x: Clarifies the change in conscious state: found on the floor this evening, confused, barely speaking, cannot open her eyes to talk. Asks about a fall or head injury (none) and about tablets or alcohol tonight (home all evening, nothing missing).
Asks about her diabetes and the risk factors for DKA:

kids.x: Type 1 diabetes since 12, on NovoMix twice daily
Insulin omission: skipping doses to lose weight, probably no dose this morning
Control: HbA1c 9% at the GP 3 weeks ago

check.x: Asks about osmotic and constitutional symptoms: thirst, large volumes of urine, tiredness and weight loss.
Screens for infection as a cause or a trigger:

kids.x: Sick contacts at school; fever, runny nose or cough (none)

kids.d: Infection, including UTI, is a common trigger of DKA, so screen for it and dipstick the urine.

kids.x: Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain all over; no diarrhoea or change in bowels; no travel or suspect food

check.x: Screens for the other causes of vomiting in an adolescent girl: medication changes including steroids (none), sexual activity as far as Celine knows (none), and her last menstrual period (2 weeks ago).
Takes the past history, medications and allergies: type 1 diabetes since 12, appendicectomy at 14, NovoMix twice daily only, no known allergies.
Takes the family history: mother with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, sister with coeliac disease, no other type 1 diabetes.
check.d: Credit noting this clustering of autoimmune disease.

check.x: Takes the social history: Year 9, more stressed lately with friendship-group problems; lives with mum and sister, more arguments at home; occasional alcohol; no smoking or drugs.

States they would do a HEEADSSS assessment with Sasha alone once she is well enough, with confidentiality explained, covering body image and eating, how she feels about her diabetes, mood and alcohol.
Explores Celine's ideas, concerns and expectations: she thinks it is the school bug, she is worried it is something serious, and she wants help now.
Examination
Asks for the full set of vital signs and identifies the rapid, deep breathing (RR 38) and the tachycardia (HR 142) with a normal BP and no fever, and gets the bedside glucose (22.0) and ketone (5.3).
Assesses the conscious level formally with GCS (13: E3 V4 M6) and the pupils, and looks for focal neurological signs (none).
Assesses hydration and perfusion (dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries) and asks for her weight (48 kg).
check.d: The weight is needed to calculate the fluids and insulin.

check.x: Recognises deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing and acetone on the breath, and auscultates the chest (clear) and heart.
Examines the abdomen: soft, mildly tender all over with no guarding or rebound, healed laparoscopic scars, renal angles not tender.
Looks for infection and other causes of drowsiness: neck stiffness, rash, ears and throat, and signs of head injury (all absent).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 38 and HR 142 to 144 in the red zone mandate a rapid response; the reduced conscious level (AVPU V, GCS 13) and family concern add to it. In the ED that means immediate senior review in resus. A normal BP and a CRT of 2 seconds mean she is not shocked.
Reads the gas: acidaemia (pH 7.25) with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HCO3 9, AG about 23) and appropriate respiratory compensation (pCO2 21).
check.d: Credit, do not require: normal oxygenation, normal lactate, Winter's formula (predicted pCO2 about 21.5, range 19.5 to 23.5); hypocapnia beyond the level expected is a cerebral oedema risk factor.

check.x: Interprets the sodium and potassium:

kids.x: Corrects the sodium for the glucose (about 133 to 134 mmol/L)
kids.d: Credit only: the corrected sodium should rise as the glucose falls.

kids.x: States that a normal potassium (4.5) hides a total-body deficit and will fall once insulin starts

check.x: Notes no infection source on the dipstick (no leucocytes or nitrites) and a negative beta-hCG.
check.d: Credit only: raised urea and creatinine as dehydration; raised WCC common in DKA with a normal CRP.

check.x: Diagnoses diabetic ketoacidosis and justifies it with the criteria (glucose above 11, pH below 7.3 or HCO3 below 15, ketonaemia). Grades it as moderate on HCO3 9 (below 10), with pH 7.25, and recognises it as high-risk and managed like severe DKA because her GCS is 13. Triggered by missed insulin.
check.d: Credit moderate, moderate to severe, or severe if justified by the reduced GCS. The critical elements are the diagnosis, the criteria and recognising it as high-risk.

check.x: Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case, including cerebral oedema. Others: gastroenteritis, UTI or pyelonephritis as a trigger, meningitis or encephalitis, and ingestion or intoxication.
Management

Resus bay, ABC, continuous monitoring, 2 IV cannulae, head up, nil by mouth; hourly BGL, neuro obs and fluid balance with gas, UEC and ketones every 2–4 h; senior ED, paediatric and PICU involvement with admission to PICU/HDU.
check.d: Critical elements: resus or monitored bed with continuous monitoring, hourly neurological observations and BGL, and PICU involvement. Credit the other elements but do not require them all.

check.x: Prescribes fluids following the RCH guideline: no bolus because she is not shocked (a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus only if shocked), and the deficit plus maintenance replaced evenly over 48 hours with 0.9% sodium chloride. Avoids rapid rehydration.
check.d: RCH: bolus only if shocked. Also credit a single 10–20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride (or balanced crystalloid) bolus over 20–30 minutes for dehydration without shock, as allowed by ISPAD 2022, if it is counted in the total and the deficit is replaced over 24–48 hours (RCH: 48 hours). Do not credit repeated boluses without shock, boluses above 20 mL/kg, or rehydration over less than 24 hours.

check.x: Adds potassium to the fluids once the potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L and she is passing urine, e.g. 40 mmol/L potassium chloride in the rehydration fluid (per RCH / local protocol).

Starts an IV short-acting insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h (2.4 to 4.8 units/h at 48 kg) about 1 hour after IV fluids have begun, with no bolus. Adds glucose to the fluids when the BGL falls below 15 mmol/L, keeps the insulin running until the acidosis resolves, and gives no bicarbonate.
check.d: Critical elements: IV insulin infusion at 0.05–0.1 units/kg/h, started about 1 hour after fluids begin, with no bolus. Credit, do not require: glucose added when the BGL is below 15, continuing until the acidosis resolves, no bicarbonate.

check.x: Recognises the GCS of 13 as high-risk for cerebral oedema now: discusses with the consultant and PICU, has mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg (24–48 g) or 3% sodium chloride 2.5–5 mL/kg (120–240 mL) ready at the bedside to give for any neurological deterioration or on senior advice, keeps the head raised and keeps fluids at the cautious 48-hour rate.
check.d: Critical elements: recognising the reduced GCS as high-risk, hyperosmolar therapy at a correct dose ready now for deterioration or on senior advice, and cautious fluids. Credit, do not require: the clinical signs that prompt immediate treatment (a fall in GCS or fluctuating conscious level, abnormal motor or verbal response to pain, decorticate or decerebrate posturing, a cranial nerve palsy or pupil change, an abnormal breathing pattern, an inappropriate fall in heart rate with rising BP; a headache or vomiting alone prompts immediate review, not treatment); reducing fluids by one-third if cerebral oedema is diagnosed; neuroimaging only after stabilisation. The ISPAD bedside criteria are for use after treatment starts.

check.x: Explains to Celine in plain words: without enough insulin the body burns fat and makes acids (ketones) and loses fluid. It is not a bug. It is serious but treatable with a drip and insulin, and no one is to blame. Checks her understanding, and asks her to tell the nurse at once if Sasha has a headache or becomes sleepier or more confused.
check.d: Critical elements: a plain-language explanation that missing insulin caused acid build-up (not a bug), an honest statement that it is serious but treatable, and telling Celine to alert the nurse at once for headache or increasing sleepiness. Credit the no-blame statement and the understanding check.

check.x: Safety netting

Asks the nurses for hourly neurological observations and an immediate call to the doctor for at least 3 warning signs of cerebral oedema: headache, irritability or new confusion, recurrent vomiting, falling GCS, slowing heart rate, rising BP, pupil changes, incontinence.
check.d: Also credit escalation for any red-zone observation, a falling potassium or a low or rapidly falling glucose.

check.x: Arranges at least 2 follow-up steps before discharge: HEEADSSS with Sasha alone; diabetes team review and re-education (sick-day plan, ketone testing, insulin regimen); psychology or adolescent medicine for insulin omission and possible disordered eating; GP follow-up.

part2.lead: Here are Sasha's observations, her arterial blood gas, her blood results and a urine dipstick.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Celine's question. React to the answer:

  • Be tearful. If the candidate explains clearly and kindly, settle a little and ask: “Is this because she's been skipping her insulin? Is it my fault?”
  • If the candidate blames Sasha or lectures you, go quiet.
  • If the candidate uses jargon (ketoacidosis, cerebral oedema, HEEADSSS), ask: “What does that mean?”

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Paediatric observation chart (12 years and over). Triage set at 19:45 and the nurse's repeat set at 20:25, both on room air. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6) at 20:25.
handover.model:
• Read: at 19:45, RR 38 with deep, sighing breaths and HR 142 are both in the red zone. AVPU is V (responds only to voice), an abnormal conscious level. Family concern is recorded. SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/70, temperature 36.8 °C and CRT 2 seconds are within normal limits. BGL 22.0. At 20:25 nothing has improved: HR 144 (red), RR 38 (red), still AVPU V with GCS 13, and she has vomited again.
  • Meaning: the high RR is Kussmaul breathing, respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not lung disease. The tachycardia reflects dehydration and acidosis. A normal BP and CRT mean she is not shocked, so no fluid bolus. Her drowsiness may be from the DKA itself, but cerebral oedema has to be considered from the start.
  • Changes: RR 38 and HR 142–144 in the red zone mandate a rapid response; the reduced conscious level (AVPU V, GCS 13) and family concern add to it. In the ED that means immediate senior review in resus, with continuous monitoring, hourly neurological observations and early PICU involvement.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: drowsy, vomiting, deep sighing breathing. Bedside ketone 5.3 mmol/L. Weight 48 kg
Repeat set: vomited about 50 mL, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), mum very worried

handover.label: Arterial blood gas
handover.result: Arterial sample, 19:55, on room air. Electrolytes, glucose and lactate measured on the gas analyser.
handover.model:
• Read: pO2 98, so oxygenation is normal. pH 7.25, acidaemia. HCO3 9 and BE −16 make it a primary metabolic acidosis. Anion gap 128 − (96 + 9) = 23, raised. Lactate 1.6 is normal, so the gap is from ketones. Compensation by Winter's formula (1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2) predicts a pCO2 of about 21.5 (19.5 to 23.5); the measured pCO2 is 21. Na 128, K 4.5, glucose 22.0.
  • Meaning: a high anion gap ketoacidosis with hyperglycaemia. HCO3 9 (below 10) makes it moderate DKA, with pH 7.25; her reduced GCS makes her high-risk. A pCO2 of 21 sits within the predicted range, so respiratory compensation is appropriate with no second disorder: the low pCO2 is her Kussmaul breathing. Hypocapnia beyond the level expected for the acidosis is a risk factor for cerebral oedema; hers is appropriate, but her reduced GCS still warrants close neurological observation. In practice a venous gas is enough in DKA; an arterial sample is shown here for practice.
  • Changes: treat as high-risk DKA. Repeat the gas with UEC and ketones every 2 to 4 hours, and involve PICU.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 19:55 at cannulation. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file at this hospital.
handover.model:
• Read: blood ketone (beta-hydroxybutyrate) 5.3, markedly raised. Urea 9.6 and creatinine 92, raised. WCC 16.8 with neutrophilia, CRP 3 (normal). Hb and platelets normal. Serum beta-hCG below 2, negative.
  • Meaning: glucose above 11, pH below 7.3 (HCO3 below 15) and ketonaemia meet the criteria for DKA. The low sodium is mostly dilutional from the hyperglycaemia. Corrected sodium is about 133 to 134 mmol/L (about 134 by the ISPAD formula Na + 2 × [(glucose − 5.6) ÷ 5.6]; about 133 by the RCH formula Na + 0.3 × (glucose − 5.5)), and it should rise as the glucose falls; a falling corrected sodium is a warning sign of cerebral oedema. A normal potassium hides a total-body deficit, and the potassium will fall once insulin starts. The raised urea and creatinine reflect dehydration (ketones can also falsely raise the measured creatinine). A raised WCC is common in DKA and is not proof of infection, and the CRP is normal. She is not pregnant.
  • Changes: 0.9% sodium chloride over 48 hours, potassium added once below 5.5 and she is passing urine, and UEC and ketones repeated every 2 to 4 hours. No antibiotics unless a source of infection appears.

rows.n: ketones may interfere with the creatinine assay

handover.label: Urine dipstick
handover.result: Urine passed at 20:10 (large volume), collected in a bedpan; bedside dipstick.
handover.model:
• Read: glucose 4+ and ketones 3+. No leucocytes, nitrites, blood or protein. SG 1.025.
  • Meaning: glycosuria and ketonuria fit DKA and explain her polyuria (an osmotic diuresis). There is no evidence of a UTI (no leucocytes or nitrites). This matters because infection is a recognised trigger of DKA. She is passing urine, so potassium can be added to the fluids.
  • Changes: no antibiotics for a urinary source. Strict fluid balance, counting the ongoing urine losses.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sasha, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sasha now, here in the emergency department.
Celine asks you, “Why has this happened, and is she going to be OK?” Please answer her, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for and what follow-up Sasha needs.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Sasha, 15.
  • Situation: moderate DKA by biochemistry with a reduced conscious level, GCS 13, so high-risk; requesting urgent review and PICU admission.
  • Background: type 1 diabetes since 12 on NovoMix twice daily, skipping insulin to lose weight, HbA1c 9%; thirst, polyuria and weight loss; 3 vomits tonight, found on the floor confused.
  • Assessment: RR 38 and HR 144 red zone, not shocked; glucose 22, ketones 5.3, pH 7.25, HCO3 9, AG 23, appropriately compensated; corrected Na about 134; K 4.5 normal but total-body deficit, will fall with insulin; dipstick shows no infection; hCG negative.
  • Recommendation: starting RCH DKA fluids, then an insulin infusion; please review now; at risk of cerebral oedema.

Diabetic ketoacidosis, moderate on HCO3 9 (below 10), with pH 7.25, and high-risk because of GCS 13, triggered by insulin omission. Supporting features: missed doses, HbA1c 9%, thirst, polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, glucose 22, ketones 5.3 and a high anion gap acidosis.

  • Cerebral oedema (must not miss): for: GCS 13 with only moderate acidosis (pH 7.25) and normal effective osmolality (278), raised urea; against: no headache, bradycardia, hypertension or pupil change; pCO2 appropriately compensated (no excess hypocapnia).
  • Gastroenteritis: for: bug at school; against: no diarrhoea or fever.
  • UTI or pyelonephritis as a trigger: against: no dysuria, dipstick negative for infection.
  • Meningitis or encephalitis: against: afebrile, no neck stiffness or rash, CRP normal.
  • Ingestion or intoxication: for: stress, alcohol at parties; against: home all evening.

1. Resus bay: ABC, continuous monitoring, 2 IV cannulae, head up, nil by mouth; hourly BGL, GCS and fluid balance, gas, UEC and ketones every 2 to 4 hours; senior ED, paediatric and PICU input; admit PICU or HDU with the diabetes team.
  2. Fluids (RCH): not shocked, so no bolus (10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride only if shocked); deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours with 0.9% sodium chloride. Also credit a single 10–20 mL/kg bolus over 20–30 min per ISPAD 2022, counted in the total.
  3. Potassium once K is below 5.5 and she is passing urine, e.g. 40 mmol/L potassium chloride in the rehydration fluid (per RCH / local protocol); credit any appropriate stated concentration.
  4. Insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h (2.4 to 4.8 units/h) about 1 hour after fluids begin, no bolus. Glucose when BGL below 15. Continue until acidosis resolves. No bicarbonate.
  5. Possible cerebral oedema now: discuss with the consultant and PICU; mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg (24–48 g) or 3% NaCl 2.5–5 mL/kg (120–240 mL) ready at the bedside for deterioration; head up; cautious fluids.

• To Celine: without insulin her body burns fat and makes acids called ketones, and she has lost a lot of fluid. It is not a bug, and it is serious but treatable with a drip and insulin. Tell the nurse at once if she gets a headache or becomes sleepier.
  • “Is it my fault?”: no one is to blame; the team will help the whole family.
  • Nurses: hourly neurological observations; call at once for headache, new confusion or irritability, recurrent vomiting, or a falling GCS or slowing HR.
  • Follow-up: diabetes team review with re-education and a sick-day plan; HEEADSSS with Sasha alone, with psychology for the insulin omission and possible disordered eating.

ddx.dx: Diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by insulin omission
ddx.for: Type 1 diabetes with doses skipped to lose weight, HbA1c 9%, thirst, polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, glucose 22, ketones 5.3 and a high anion gap acidosis with pH 7.25.
GCS 13 with only moderate acidosis (pH 7.25) and normal effective osmolality (278), raised urea.
ddx.against: No headache, bradycardia, hypertension, pupil change or focal signs; pCO2 appropriately compensated (no excess hypocapnia); drowsiness can come from the DKA itself. But her effective osmolality is normal (2 × 128 + 22 = 278 mOsm/kg) and her acidosis is only moderate, so a GCS of 13 is not fully explained: treat as possible cerebral oedema and reassess the GCS hourly.

ddx.for: There is a bug going around her school and she has vomited three times.
ddx.against: No diarrhoea or fever, she has days of thirst and polyuria, and the glucose and ketones explain her illness.

ddx.dx: Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis triggering DKA
ddx.for: Infection, including UTI, is a common trigger of DKA, and she has vomiting and abdominal pain.
ddx.against: No dysuria or loin pain, she is afebrile, and the dipstick shows no leucocytes or nitrites.

ddx.for: She is drowsy, confused and vomiting, with sick contacts at school.
ddx.against: She is afebrile with no neck stiffness or rash, the CRP is normal, and DKA explains the drowsiness.

ddx.for: She is a stressed adolescent with friendship problems who drinks at parties and was found drowsy on the floor.
ddx.against: She was home all evening, no tablets are missing, and the glucose, ketones and gas explain her conscious state.

guide:
In Part 1 the person playing Celine answers the history and gives each detail only when asked. The examiner voices Sasha's few mumbled words and gives findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse gives the triage observations, and gives the bedside glucose and ketone only when they are asked for. The nurse reports the further vomit partway through. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, say “Noted, please cover it in Part 2”, and credit early recognition and escalation under Professionalism. If they ask for a gas, bloods or a urine sample, say the results come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the gas, the bloods and the dipstick, then ask all four questions in order. Read Celine's question aloud to open question 4. She asks her one follow-up question while the candidate answers. The candidate must calculate the anion gap; it is not printed on the gas. In question 4, any 3 warning signs for the nurses and any 2 follow-up steps earn the marks.

Changes from the source case: the source prints the urine dipstick as “NAD”, which cannot fit a glucose of 22 with polyuria. Here the dipstick shows glucose and ketones and keeps the source's point that there is no evidence of a UTI. The source's pH of 7.1 has been adjusted to 7.25 so that the compensation matches her Kussmaul breathing; HCO3 9 is moderate on the RCH grading (moderate is pH below 7.2 or HCO3 below 10; severe is pH below 7.1 or HCO3 below 5). Credit moderate, moderate to severe, or severe if justified by her reduced GCS, as long as the candidate treats her as high-risk. The arterial gas is kept for practice; credit a candidate who says a venous gas is enough in DKA.

A high-performing candidate gets a bedside glucose and ketone and senior help within the first minute or two. They elicit the insulin omission, the osmotic symptoms and the weight loss, screen for infection, injury and ingestion, and say they will do a HEEADSSS assessment with Sasha alone later. They measure the GCS and weight. In Part 2 they read the gas systematically with the anion gap and compensation, correct the sodium and explain the hidden potassium deficit. They give slow fluids over 48 hours without a bolus, add potassium once it is below 5.5 and she is passing urine, and start an insulin infusion about 1 hour after the fluids without a bolus. They admit to PICU, know the warning signs of cerebral oedema and its immediate treatment, and explain kindly to Celine without blame.

A borderline candidate takes a gastroenteritis history and misses the insulin omission, or never asks for a glucose. They may call the potassium “normal, so no replacement”, give repeated boluses without shock or an insulin bolus, or forget the neurological observations.
explain:
Diagnosis: diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by insulin omission

Sasha is 15 and has had type 1 diabetes since she was 12. She has several days of thirst, polyuria, tiredness and weight loss. Tonight she vomited three times and was found drowsy and confused. She has deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, acetone on her breath, tachycardia and clinical dehydration, with a normal BP. The trigger is in the history: she has been skipping insulin to lose weight, and her HbA1c was 9%. The RCH guideline defines DKA as:

  • hyperglycaemia (BGL above 11 mmol/L);
  • a venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L;
  • ketonaemia (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 3 mmol/L or more) or moderate to large ketonuria.

ISPAD 2022 uses HCO3 below 18 mmol/L; follow your local guideline.

Severity is graded on the pH and bicarbonate. Mild is pH below 7.3 or HCO3 below 15. Moderate is pH below 7.2 or HCO3 below 10. Severe is pH below 7.1 or HCO3 below 5. Sasha's pH of 7.25 alone would be mild, but her HCO3 of 9 (below 10) makes her moderate; her reduced conscious level makes her high-risk, with ICU involvement.

Vomiting in children and adolescents

  • Check a glucose and ketones in any vomiting or drowsy child with diabetes. DKA is also the first presentation of type 1 diabetes in a proportion of children.
  • Be cautious about diagnosing gastroenteritis when there is vomiting without diarrhoea; look for another cause.
  • In a vomiting infant or young child, treat a UTI as present until proven otherwise and dipstick the urine. At any age, infection, including UTI, is a common trigger of DKA, so screen for it.
  • Assess dehydration: mucous membranes, perfusion, weight and, in younger children, wet nappies.
  • Age changes the differentials. In a younger child, add birth, feeding, growth, development, maternal and child health nurse concerns, sick contacts and whether they are their usual self. Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks (typically 3 to 6) suggests pyloric stenosis.
  • In adolescents, ask the parents about their concerns, then do a HEEADSSS assessment with the young person alone.

Interpreting the blood gas

Use a systematic approach:

  1. Oxygenation: pO2 98 on room air is normal.
  2. pH: 7.25, acidaemia.
  3. Primary disturbance: HCO3 9 and BE −16 make it metabolic. The pCO2 is low, not high, so the problem is not respiratory.
  4. Anion gap: Na − (Cl + HCO3) = 128 − (96 + 9) = 23, raised. A high gap points to lactate, toxins, ketones or renal failure. A normal gap points to diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis or saline. With a normal lactate and a ketone of 5.3, this is ketoacidosis.
  5. Compensation: Winter's formula (1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2) predicts a pCO2 of about 21.5 (19.5 to 23.5). Her pCO2 of 21 is within this range, so the respiratory compensation is appropriate and there is no second disorder: the low pCO2 is her Kussmaul breathing. Hypocapnia, especially beyond the level expected for the acidosis, is a recognised risk factor for cerebral oedema.

A venous gas is enough for diagnosis and monitoring in DKA. The arterial sample here is for practice.

Electrolytes and other results

  • Sodium: hyperglycaemia draws water into the blood and dilutes the sodium. Correct it: Na + 2 × [(glucose − 5.6) ÷ 5.6] gives about 134 mmol/L (the RCH formula, Na + 0.3 × (glucose − 5.5), gives about 133). The corrected sodium should rise as the glucose falls. If it falls, think of cerebral oedema.
  • Potassium: the total-body potassium is depleted by the osmotic diuresis and vomiting, even when the serum level is normal. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so the level falls once treatment starts.
  • Urea and creatinine: raised from dehydration; ketones can also interfere with some creatinine assays.
  • WCC: a raised count is common in DKA from stress and is not proof of infection. Look for a source clinically.
  • Beta-hCG: check it in an adolescent girl, with appropriate confidentiality.

Management (RCH Diabetic ketoacidosis guideline)

  • Setting: resuscitation bay, ABC, continuous monitoring, 2 IV lines and the head of the bed raised. Severe DKA or a reduced conscious level needs ICU involvement.
  • Fluids: shock is uncommon. Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus only if she is shocked. Otherwise replace the deficit plus maintenance slowly and evenly over 48 hours with 0.9% sodium chloride, calculated from her weight. Rapid rehydration is avoided because of the risk of cerebral oedema. ISPAD 2022 allows 10–20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 20–30 minutes for a dehydrated child who is not shocked, and replaces the deficit over 24–48 hours; follow your local guideline.
  • Potassium: add it to the fluids once the potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L and she is passing urine (for example 40 mmol/L potassium chloride in the rehydration fluid, per RCH or local protocol).
  • Insulin: an IV short-acting insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, started about 1 hour after IV fluids have begun, with no bolus. Add glucose to the fluids when the BGL falls below about 15 mmol/L, and continue the insulin until the ketoacidosis has resolved. Bicarbonate is not given.
  • Nil by mouth while she is drowsy and vomiting.
  • Monitoring: hourly BGL, neurological observations and fluid balance; UEC, gas and ketones every 2 to 4 hours.
  • Find the cause: here, missed insulin.

Cerebral oedema

Cerebral oedema is the main cause of death from DKA in children. It usually occurs in the first hours of treatment, but it can be present at presentation. Risk factors:

  • young age and a new diagnosis;
  • severe acidosis, and greater hypocapnia than expected for the degree of acidosis;
  • a raised urea;
  • bicarbonate treatment;
  • large or rapid fluid volumes;
  • a corrected sodium that does not rise.

Warning signs are headache, irritability or behaviour change, recurrent vomiting, a falling conscious level, a slowing heart rate with rising BP, pupil changes and incontinence. If it is suspected, act at once. The ISPAD bedside criteria are applied once treatment has started (signs present before treatment do not count), but Sasha's GCS of 13 may not be fully explained by a moderate acidosis with a normal effective osmolality, so treatment is discussed with PICU now and hyperosmolar therapy kept ready at the bedside:

  • reduce the fluid rate by one-third;
  • give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 20 minutes or 3% sodium chloride 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes;
  • keep the head raised;
  • call PICU.

The cause: insulin omission in an adolescent

Deliberately skipping insulin to lose weight is a recognised form of disordered eating in young women with type 1 diabetes. Sasha has several clues: the weight loss, school and friendship stress, arguments at home and alcohol. Once she is well, she needs a HEEADSSS assessment (Home, Education and employment, Eating and exercise, Activities, Drugs and alcohol, Sexuality, Suicide and mood, Safety), done alone with confidentiality explained. It should cover body image, eating behaviours and how she feels about her diabetes. The diabetes team (including psychology) supports her with re-education, a sick-day plan, ketone testing and possibly a change of insulin regimen. Her family history of Hashimoto's and coeliac disease reflects the clustering of autoimmune disease with type 1 diabetes.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, the nurses and Celine report any headache, new irritability or confusion, further vomiting or a falling conscious level at once. The team also watches for hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia as treatment works. Before discharge she needs HEEADSSS with Sasha alone, diabetes team education, psychology or adolescent medicine follow-up, and GP review. The family is told to return to the ED (or call 000 if she is very drowsy) for vomiting, high blood ketones, abdominal pain or deep breathing.

Read a gas systematically: oxygenation, pH, primary disturbance, anion gap, then compensation (Winter's formula). DKA is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
